title: Mechanic
wiki_lead:
A mechanic is a skilled tradesperson who uses tools, procedures, and experiential knowledge to build, alter, maintain, repair, restore, test, or improve the capabilities of machinery, especially vehicles or other mechanical devices. The term previously referred to anyone in various handicraft trades, but it has referred specifically to those who work with machinery since the early 20th century. A technician is generally a mechanic who, through higher education, experience, or a non-proficiency-based title, engages in performance or instruction of more nuanced, technically challenging operations, and generally has a greater understanding of a system's operations and specifications.
Mechanics work across a wide range of disciplines, including automotive, energy, maritime, aeronautical, civil, domestic, mining, military, industrial, agricultural, and pharmaceutical. The responsibilities typically include inspecting equipment, diagnosing faults, setting parameters of moving assemblies, adjusting flow and pressures of fluid systems, verifying proper installation of new components if installed by secondary entities, and repairing or replacing components. They perform preventive maintenance to ensure machinery operates safely and efficiently. The profession developed rapidly during the Industrial Revolution, when increasing mechanisation created demand for specialised technical skills.
Training generally involves practical experience and apprenticeship, although vocational education, formal qualifications, and professional certification have become requirements in many fields. The modern mechanic works increasingly with electrical systems, computerised diagnostics, and advanced maintenance techniques, but generally will not directly work to fix problems associated with electronic, digital, or high-precision applications, as these specialties are pursued by electricians, computer scientists, and machinists. The occupation involves workplace hazards, including exposure to noise and chemicals, the danger of moving machinery, and risk of physical strain. It may involve working with, or to written instruction from: engineers, OEMs, customers, federal or state requirements, architects, designers, planners, testers, inspectors, or any body that may have authority or jurisdiction over the mechanic's task.

Etymology
The word mechanic is derived from Middle French mécanique, originating from Latin mechanicus, borrowed from Ancient Greek μηχανικός (mēkhanikós; 'of machines, mechanical'), from μηχανή (mēkhanḗ; 'machine, device') with the suffix -ικός (-ikós; 'relating to'). 
The word appeared in the Middle English poem Confessio Amantis, by John Gower, written in the late 14th century, spelt originally as mechanique, with the connotation of artisanry (a translation of the Latin term ars mechanica). grok_lead: A mechanic is a skilled tradesperson who diagnoses, repairs, and maintains mechanical equipment, such as engines, vehicles, and industrial machinery. Mechanics typically work in automotive repair shops, factories, or service centers, using specialized tools and diagnostic software to identify issues and perform fixes ranging from routine maintenance like oil changes to complex overhauls of transmissions or electrical systems. The profession demands physical stamina, as workers often lift heavy parts, work in noisy or greasy environments, and may face high rates of on-the-job injuries compared to other occupations. Mechanics specialize in various areas, including automotive service for cars and light trucks, diesel technicians for heavy vehicles, heavy equipment technicians for construction and agricultural machinery, and industrial mechanics for factory equipment. Entry into the field usually requires a high school diploma followed by postsecondary training, such as a certificate or associate degree in automotive technology, though some gain skills through apprenticeships or on-the-job experience. Certifications from organizations like the National Institute for Automotive Service Excellence (ASE) enhance employability and are often required for tasks involving refrigerants or advanced diagnostics. In the United States, as of May 2024, the median annual wage for automotive service technicians and mechanics was $49,670, with employment projected to grow 4% from 2024 to 2034, about as fast as the average for all occupations, due to more vehicles on the road and the need to maintain complex safety features, although the rise of electric vehicles may limit some demand.
